question: Directions: Read the following passage to answer the given questions based on it. Some words/phrases are printed in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions. (The passage has been extracted from 'The Hindu' dated June 11, 2014.) Ever since the morning after 26/11, India’s strategic community has discussed what the country ought to do when the next 26/11 happens. Prime Minister Narendra Modi may have to answer that question sooner than most people expect. The Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) staged its first operation against an Indian target since 26/11 just hours before Mr. Modi took office, attacking India’s mission in Herat. Lashkar chief Hafiz Muhammad Saeed blamed Mr. Modi for this week’s attacks on Karachi — and demanded vengeance. From past evidence, we know these threats aren’t idle . “The only language India understands is that of force,” a press release issued by the Lashkar’s parent organisation, Jamaat-ud-Dawa recorded Mr. Saeed as saying before 26/11, “and that is the language it must be talked to in.” From files he will have read since taking office, Mr. Modi will have learned why Dr. Singh did nothing. Indian combat jets could hit training camps across the Line of Control (LoC), Air Chief Marshal Fali Major said at a November 29 meeting called for by the Prime Minister, but precise coordinates and adequate imaging weren’t available. Later, General Deepak Kapoor, the chief of Army staff, told Dr. Singh he couldn’t promise special forces’ strikes would be successful either. No one could guarantee missile strikes wouldn’t escalate into war, or even a nuclear exchange — and no one could guarantee war would compel Pakistan’s military to change course. Mr. Modi’s advisers know five responses are on the table — but all of them involve great risks. The first is to keep doing nothing. The threat of a major India- Pakistan crisis after 26/11 led the United States to mount intense pressure on Pakistan. In the years since, the LeT hasn’t mounted a single major operation on Indian soil. Its affiliate, the Indian Mujahideen, has had restraint thrust upon it by Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) Directorate. Inaction, though, only succeeds if someone else does the hard work. In 2008, fearing its own war in Afghanistan would be undermined by an India-Pakistan war, the U.S. stepped in. Now, as it prepares to withdraw from Afghanistan, the country’s appetite for playing global policeman is diminishing. Doing nothing could thus invite even more punishment. Like Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, Mr. Modi’s second choice might be coercion. In 2001, after terrorists attacked Parliament, India mobilised troops. Pakistan was forced to respond — but its smaller economy suffered disproportionately. The stratagem is time-tested. In 1953, Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru mobilised troops in Punjab to deter a Pakistani attack into Kashmir. Mr. Vajpayee’s strategy worked, forcing Pakistan to dramatically scale down the jihad in Jammu and Kashmir. It only worked, though, because the U.S. played mediator — much like after 26/11 — and it was hideously expensive, in money and lives. The third choice is to do what Dr. Singh couldn’t: limited strikes on jihadist training camps across the LoC, using air power or missiles. In the five years since 26/11, India’s ability to conduct such strikes has been significantly enhanced. However, the tactic hasn’t had great success. In August 1998, the United States fired missiles into Afghanistan, seeking to avenge bombings which killed 224 people. In all, 75 missiles, each priced at $1.5 million, killed six minor jihadists. Moreover, Pakistan could hit back, targeting Indian industrial infrastructure, which is much more expensive than tent-and-donkey cart training camps. Fourth, the Prime Minister could tell Indian troops to target the Pakistan Army along the LoC, using artillery and infantry — a task aided by the fact that its defences along stretches of the Neelam valley have been degraded by troops having to be moved to fight the Tehreek-e-Taliban elsewhere. The fighting that will follow though will make it more difficult to secure the LoC against jihadist infiltration — leading to heightened violence in Kashmir. Mr. Modi could, finally, authorise the use of covert means, like bomb-for-bomb strikes or targeted assassination of jihadist leaders. Mr. Modi’s intelligence services, though, don’t have this arrow in their quiver — and it will be a while, most experts say, before they can acquire it. Every sane person should hope Mr. Modi will never be required to exercise any of his military options — but thinking through war is just as important as talking peace. 1. What is the major reason according to the passage is for the Lashkar-e-Taiba not mounting a major operation on Indian soil after 26/11?
options: Due to India's enhanced security after 26/11
Due to India's serious dialogue with Pakistan
Due to the pressure Pakistan got from the United States of America
Because the outfit lost its Chief in an accident
answer: Option C: Due to the pressure Pakistan got from the United States of America
solution: Correct Answer: Option C: Due to the pressure Pakistan got from the United States of America. Solved following standard Infosys System Engineer evaluation criteria.

question:
Fill in the blank with a suitable word from the options.

After centuries of obscurity, this philosopher’s thesis is enjoying a surprising ____ .
solution: Ans - D The sentence tells us that the thesis has been in obscurity (forgotten or neglected) but now it is being revived. We can say it is undergoing a renaissance (revival).

question:
Fill in the blank with suitable words from the options.

There is a general ____ in the United States that our ethics are declining and that our moral standards are ____.
solution: Ans - D The conjunction ‘and’ usually joins things of similar meaning or weight. This suggests that since ethics are declining, moral standards are also declining (deteriorating). Almost any word except ‘optimism’ would have fit the first blank.

question:
Fill in the blank with suitable words from the options.

In the Middle Ages, the ____ of the great cathedrals did not enter into the architects’ plans; almost invariably a cathedral was positioned haphazardly in ____ surroundings.
solution: Ans - A The semicolon indicates that the second part of the sentence expands on the first part. So, the second part tells us we are talking about the position, or situation of a cathedral. And since the first part tells us that architects did not pay attention to the situation, the cathedral was positioned randomly in odd (incongruous) surroundings.

question: The quantum theory was initially regarded as absurd, unnatural and ____ with common sense.
solution: Ans - C A set of words linked with ‘and’ usually indicates things of similar weight. To go with ‘absurd’ and ‘unnatural’ we can choose incompatible with common sense.

question: Abraham Lincoln was famously known for his ______, which explains why he is often referred to as “Honest Abe.”
solution: Ans - C Here, the keyword is “honest,” and the missing word is used to explain why Lincoln was called honest. Thus, the missing word must also mean honesty, as only someone known for honesty would be called “honest.”, As veracity means honesty or truthfulness, it’s the suitable answer.

question:
Fill in the blanks with suitable answer options.

Archaeology is a poor profession; only ____ sums are available for excavating sites and even more ____ amounts for preserving the excavations.
solution: Ans - A The part after the semicolon expands upon the first part of the sentence. So, since the first part tells us that there is no money in archaeology, then there will only be small (paltry) amounts for excavating. Also ‘even more’ indicates that another similar word is required. Thus, meager also means small.

question: The village headman was unlettered, but he was no fool, he could see through the ________ of the businessman’s proposition and promptly _______ him down.
solution: Ans - D The sentence suggests that although the village headman was illiterate, he was wise. This information must have been provided in order to validate that he could see through the deception (sophistry) of the businessman’s proposition and must have turned him down.

question: Moths are nocturnal pollinators, visiting scented flowers during the hours of darkness, whereas the butterflies are ____ , attracted to bright flowers in the daytime.
solution: Ans - A ‘Whereas’ indicates opposite ideas. So we need a word in contrast to ‘nocturnal’ (active at night). The word is diurnal (active in daytime).

question: War has been, throughout history, the chief _________ of social cohesion; and since science began, it has been the strongest ________ to technical progress.
solution: Ans - D In the given space of time i.e. ’throughout history’ there can be only source. Reason and cause or origin can be a particular event. Boost, encouragement and incentive mean the same.

question: Scrooge, in the famous novel by Dickens, was a ______; he hated the rest of mankind.
solution: Ans - A The part of the sentence after the semicolon defines the word needed for the blank. So, since he ‘hated mankind’, the word we need is misanthrope (hater of the rest of mankind).

question:
Fill in the blank with a suitable word from the options.

In her crusade to make public servants accountable to voters, she________ the nation's unscrupulous and self-indulgent politicians.
solution: Ans - A If the nation's politicians had been unscrupulous and self-indulgent, and a woman crusader wanted to make them accountable to the voters, she would not have dramatized, or accepted, or foreshadowed or promoted them, but would have exposed them.

question: In a fit of ____ she threw out the valuable statue simply because it had belonged to her ex-husband.
solution: Ans - A She threw out a valuable statue just because it belonged to her ex-husband. Therefore, she must have been acting out of spite or ill will. Hence we choose pique which means ‘resentment’.

question:
Fill in the blanks with the correct answer.

In this biography we are given a glimpse of the young man ______ pursuing the path of the poet despite ______ and rejection slips.
solution: Ans - A The word ’despite’ indicates something contrary. So, despite the rejection slips he pursues his path doggedly or tirelessly. But since the ‘and’ links similar things he is getting disappointment along with the rejection slips, not encouragement.

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct answer.

The assumption that chlorofluorocarbons would be _________ in the environment because they were chemically inert, was challenged by the demonstration of a potential threat to the ozone layer.
solution: Ans - B Turn the sentence around, and fit a word of your own in the blank. The demonstration of the potential threat challenged the assumption that the CFCs would be ‘harmless’ because they were inert. Innocuous is the best word because it means harmless.

question: The professor became increasingly _______ in later years, flying into a rage whenever he was opposed.
solution: Ans - C The required word is signaled by the phrase ‘ flying into a rage’. Someone who is easily angered is described as ‘irascible’.

question: Read the passage and answer the questions. Management is a set of processes that can keep a complicated system of people and technology to run smoothly. The most important aspects of management include planning, budgeting, organizing, staffing, controlling and problem-solving. Leadership is a set of processes that creates organizations in the first place or adapts them to significantly changing circumstances. Leadership defines what the future should look like, aligns people with that vision and inspires them to make it happen despite the obstacles. This distinction is absolutely crucial for our purposes here: Successful transformation is 70 to 90 per cent leadership and only 10 to 30 percent management. Yet for historical reasons, many organizations today don't have much leadership. And almost everyone thinks about the problem here as one of managing change. For most of this country, as we created thousands and thousands of large organizations for the first time in human history, we didn't have enough good managers to keep all those bureaucracies functioning. Many companies and universities developed management programs and hundreds and thousands of people were encouraged to learn management on the job. And they did. But, people were taught little about leadership. To some degree, management was emphasized because it's easier to preach than leadership. But even more so, management was the main item on the twentieth century agenda because that's what was needed. For every entrepreneur or business builder who was a leader, we needed hundreds of managers to run their ever-growing enterprises. Unfortunately for us today, this emphasis on management has often been institutionalized in corporate cultures that discourage employees from learning how to lead. Ironically, past success is usually the key ingredient in producing this outcome. The syndrome, as I have observed it on many occasions, goes like this: Success creates some degree of marked dominance which in turn produces much growth. After a while keeping the ever-larger organization under control becomes the primary challenge. So, attention turns inward and managerial competencies are nurtured. With a strong emphasis on management but not leadership, bureaucracy and an inward focus takeover. But with continued success, the result mostly of market dominance, the problem often goes unaddressed and an unhealthy arrogance begins to evolve. All of these characteristics then make any transformation effort much more difficult. Arrogant managers can over-evaluate their current performance and competitive position, listen poorly and learn slowly. Inwardly focused employees can have difficulty seeing the very forces that present threats and opportunities. Bureaucratic cultures can smother those who want to respond to shifting conditions. And the lack of leadership leaves no force inside these organizations to break out of the morass. Q. Why did companies and universities develop programs to prepare managers in such large numbers?
options: Companies and universities wanted to generate funds through these programs.
The large number of organizations were created as they needed managers in good number.
Organizations did not want to spend their scarce resources in training managers.
Organizations wanted to create communication network through trained managers.
answer: Option B: The large number of organizations were created as they needed managers in good number.
solution: Correct Answer: Option B: The large number of organizations were created as they needed managers in good number.. Solved following standard Infosys System Engineer evaluation criteria.

question: Read the passage and answer the questions. The impressive recent growth of certain sectors of the Indian economy is a necessary but insufficient condition for the elimination of extreme poverty. In order to ensure that the poorest benefit from this growth, and also contribute to it, the expansion and improvement of the microfinance sector should be a national priority.studies suggest that the impact of microfinance on the poorest is greater than on the poor, and yet another that non-participating members of communities where microfinance operates experience socio-economic gains suggesting strong spillover effects. Moreover, well-managed microfinance institutions (MFIs) have shown a capacity to wean themselves off of subsidies and become sustainable within a few years. Microfinance is powerful, but it is clearly no panacea. Microfinance does not directly address some structural problems facing Indian society and the economy, and it is not yet as efficient as it will be when economies of scale are realised and a more supportive policy environment is created. Loan products are still too inflexible, and savings and insurance services that the poor also need are not widely available due to regulatory barriers Still, microfinance is one of the few market-based, scaleable anti-poverty solutions that is in place in India today, and the argument to scale it up to meet the overwhelming need is compelling.According to Sa-Dhan, the overall outreach is 6.5 million families and the sector-wide loan portfolio is Rs 2,500 crore. However, this is meeting only 10% of the estimated demand. Importantly, new initiatives are expanding this success story to the some of the country's poorest regions, such as eastern and central Uttar Pradesh. The local and national governments have an important role to play in ensuring the growth and improvement of microfinance. First and foremost, the market should be left to set interest rates, not the state. Ensuring transparency and full disclosure of rates including fees is something the government should ensure, and something that new technologies as well as reporting and data standards are already enabling. Furthermore, government regulators should set clear criteria for allowing MFIs to mobilise savings for on-lending to the poor; this would allow for a large measure of financial independence amongst well-managed MFIs. Each Indian state could consider forming a multi-party working group to meet with microfinance leaders and have a dialogue with them about how the policy environment could be made more supportive and to clear up misperceptions. There is an opportunity to make a real dent in hard-core poverty through microfinance. By unleashing the entrepreneurial talent of the poor, we will slowly but surely transform India in ways we can only begin to imagine today. Q. Which of following is not a challenge faced by microfinance in India?
options: fficient when economy of scale is achieved
answer: Option A: does not help the poorest
solution: Correct Answer: Option A: does not help the poorest. Solved following standard Infosys System Engineer evaluation criteria.

question: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow : Once upon a time, in a quaint little village nestled in a picturesque valley, there lived a young girl named Lily. She was known for her adventurous spirit and her deep curiosity. One sunny afternoon, while exploring the woods that bordered the village, Lily stumbled upon a hidden clearing. In the center of this secret meadow, she found an old oak tree with a peculiar nook. In that nook, half-buried in the earth, was a mysterious locket, ornate and gleaming with intricate designs. Lily carefully unearthed it, and as she held it in her hand, she felt a strange connection to this forgotten piece of jewelry. Back in her cottage, Lily examined the locket more closely. It was made of silver with a hint of gold, and its surface was adorned with delicate engravings of leaves and flowers. On the front, there was an image of a crescent moon, and on the back, an engraving read, “To the one who seeks the truth.” The locket was sealed tightly, and Lily couldn’t open it no matter how hard she tried. Determined to solve the mystery, Lily embarked on a quest to find someone who could open the locket. She asked the village blacksmith, the wise old woman who lived on the hill, and even the town’s mayor, but none of them could unlock its secrets. Feeling a bit discouraged, Lily spent her days reading about ancient relics and searching for clues in the library. One day, while immersed in an old book about mystical lockets, Lily came across a passage that mentioned the existence of a “key of the heart.” It said that this key could open the most stubborn of locks, but it was hidden within each person, waiting to be discovered. This newfound knowledge gave Lily a renewed sense of hope and determination. The next morning, Lily decided to visit the village’s recluse, an elderly woman rumored to have deep knowledge of the heart. The recluse lived in a remote cottage surrounded by a lush garden. Lily knocked on the door and explained her quest. The old woman listened attentively and finally agreed to help. She told Lily that the key to opening the locket was hidden within her heart and that she needed to meditate on her truest desires and intentions. Lily followed the recluse’s advice, sitting beneath the ancient oak tree where she had found the locket. She closed her eyes, focused on her heart’s deepest desires, and as she did, she felt the locket warming in her hand. When she opened her eyes, she found the locket had sprung open, revealing a tiny, folded parchment inside. With trembling hands, she carefully unfolded it and read the message: “The truth lies in the journey, not the destination.” The mystery of the locket was solved, but Lily realized that the real treasure was the journey of self-discovery she had undertaken. She understood that her quest had led her to understand her heart’s desires and the power of her own determination. Question 1- What did Lily discover in the hidden clearing in the woods?
answer: Option B: An old oak tree
solution: Correct Answer: Option B: An old oak tree. Solved following standard Infosys System Engineer evaluation criteria.

question:
Directions (01- 10): Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
When we are children growing up, our imagination is the key to untold worlds. And it has been shown that kids with very active imaginations are more likely to dream and strive for greater things as adults. It is a sad fact that all too often, as we grow up, we are told to “get our heads out of the clouds”, to "stop daydreaming", and that living in an imaginary world is not good for us. But stifling your imagination is the worst thing you can do to yourself, as it will only pave the way for accelerated aging, and all too often a life that feels unfulfilled.
Though many take creativity for granted, it is a trait not possessed by everyone. Many people are labelled as primarily “right brained” or “left brained” (if such a thing exists): It is argued that highly intellectual, logical types are less likely to be creative, have less wild imaginations and are typically rule followers who do not believe in much of anything that cannot be logically quantified. Regardless of the left brain / right brain argument, imagination unleashes creativity, allowing you to live a life filled with potential. The creative individual does not see the sky as the limit, instead the limit is as far as he or she can imagine. They not only think outside the box, for them there is no box, and so their brains are constantly challenged, humming and conjuring up all sorts of goodies. Anything the mind can conjure is good enough to become true, be it work, life, personal goals accomplishments or anything. A very good trait to cultivate from childhood.
Empathy is the act of being truly sympathetic to another person, without ever actually experiencing what they are going through yourself. Sadly, many people do not know how to express empathy, and the reason for this is simple; it is not because that person is a bad individual, or mean spirited. It simply means that individual cannot imagine the feelings of the person experiencing a particular event, and thus cannot truly relate. Your imagination may leave you in a good position to offer a shoulder for comfort and support, as you are able to envision going through the same thing as the person suffering, and thus able to demonstrate what you think a person needs at that time. Being of service towards other people in that way, promotes your own mental health and emotional well being.
Those brain connections are a part of what makes you who you are, and forming new connections supports memory functions and keeps the brain vibrant and strong. Your imagination can be a useful tool for strengthening these connections, in order to form long-term memories. Here are two explanations of how memory works; an intellectual will harness and strengthen memory by repetition. Studying work day after day enhances these connections bit by bit, or via physical practice. On the other hand, someone who uses their imagination may know something well, and be able to recall everything without seeming to make an effort. Take for example planning for their wedding. Years and years beforehand, that person could have meticulously planned and imagined their dream wedding, so that when the actual time comes, the planning step and what they want pops up like clockwork.

 Q1. What, according to the passage, is/are the disadvantage(s) of constraining the children to be realistic and not imaginative?

(I) it will lead to an unfulfilled life.
(II) They lack empathy
 (III) It limits the growth of their brain
solution: Refer the last few lines of first paragraph “But stifling your imagination is the worst thing you can do to yourself, as it will only pave the way for accelerated aging, and all too often a life that feels unfulfilled.” Hence option (c) is the correct choice.

And it has been shown that kids with very active imaginations are more likely to dream and strive for greater things as adults. It is a sad fact that all too often, as we grow up, we are told to “get our heads out of the clouds”, to "stop daydreaming", and that living in an imaginary world is not good for us. But stifling your imagination is the worst thing you can do to yourself, as it will only pave the way for accelerated aging, and all too often a life that feels unfulfilled.
Though many take creativity for granted, it is a trait not possessed by everyone. Many people are labelled as primarily “right brained” or “left brained” (if such a thing exists): It is argued that highly intellectual, logical types are less likely to be creative, have less wild imaginations and are typically rule followers who do not believe in much of anything that cannot be logically quantified. Regardless of the left brain / right brain argument, imagination unleashes creativity, allowing you to live a life filled with potential. The creative individual does not see the sky as the limit, instead the limit is as far as he or she can imagine. They not only think outside the box, for them there is no box, and so their brains are constantly challenged, humming and conjuring up all sorts of goodies. Anything the mind can conjure is good enough to become true, be it work, life, personal goals accomplishments or anything. A very good trait to cultivate from childhood.
 Empathy is the act of being truly sympathetic to another person, without ever actually experiencing what they are going through yourself. Sadly, many people do not know how to express empathy, and the reason for this is simple; it is not because that person is a bad individual, or mean spirited. It simply means that individual cannot imagine the feelings of the person experiencing a particular event, and thus cannot truly relate. Your imagination may leave you in a good position to offer a shoulder for comfort and support, as you are able to envision going through the same thing as the person suffering, and thus able to demonstrate what you think a person needs at that time. Being of service towards other people in that way, promotes your own mental health and emotional well being.Those brain connections are a part of what makes you who you are, and forming new connections supports memory functions and keeps the brain vibrant and strong. Your imagination can be a useful tool for strengthening these connections, in order to form long-term memories. Here are two explanations of how memory works; an intellectual will harness and strengthen memory by repetition. Studying work day after day enhances these connections bit by bit, or via physical practice. On the other hand, someone who uses their imagination may know something well, and be able to recall everything without seeming to make an effort. Take for example planning for their wedding. Years and years beforehand, that person could have meticulously planned and imagined their dream wedding, so that when the actual time comes, the planning step and what they want pops up like clockwork

options: Harmful effects of stiflings the imagination
The power of using your imagination
Imagining beyond the limit of the sky.
answer: Option B: The power of using your imagination
solution: “ The power of using your imagination” is an appropriate title of the passage as the passage revolves around the theme of advantages of being imaginative.

question:
Directions (1-5): Read the given passage and answer the following questions based on the passage.
For almost two decades, the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) has been reporting on the increasing number of over-exploited blocks across India, the ‘dark’ category blocks. The recent annual book of CGWB has reported 1,034 units, out of the 6,584 units it monitors, as over-exploited. If this is the ‘crisis’, then we have had it for long. What has this not received enough attention? Is it because these zones are not in cities?

Just to be sure how critical the ‘crisis’ is, CGWB’s 2013 estimates say that the groundwater development in India is just about 62% of the utilisable groundwater reserves. Similarly, a recent report by the Central Water Commission, prepared in collaboration with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), asserted that India is not yet in “water scarcity condition”. But it is certainly in a “water-stressed condition”, with reducing per capita water availability. Here, we certainly don’t mean to say that India can continue with the present ways of water management. We also cannot remain in a state of denial that a crisis is not in the making. However, certain steps need to be taken to ensure a more useful and productive discourse about water governance challenges.

First, India needs to reconsider the institutional processes for dissemination of knowledge about water resource management. There is a certain amount of danger inherent in the casual manner in which knowledge about water resources is legitimised and consumed, particularly in these days of ‘viral’ information.

Second, we need to recognise the crisis is not as much of scarcity as of delivery. The challenge is to ensure an adequate access to quality water, more so in urban areas where inequities over space and time are acute. We need to also realise that with the country’s rapid urbanisation, demand cannot be met by groundwater reserves alone. For instance, according to the Delhi Jal Board estimates, groundwater meets just 10% of Delhi’s drinking water needs. The rest is met by surface water sources, most of it transported from outside Delhi. The urban needs, which underpin much reporting on ‘water crises’, need to be met by robust long-term planning and preparation for droughts and other contingencies.

Finally, we need to reconsider our approaches to water governance. We must recognise that the fulcrum of change and action is with the States. For long, water resource departments in States have continued to follow the conventional approaches of supply augmentation. The challenge is that of reorienting themselves towards deploying strategies of demand management, conservation and regulation. The Centre has to work with States towards an institutional change for the necessary course-shift. The Finance Minister, in her budget, repeatedly stated that the government will work with States to address India’s national water security challenges. Let us hope that the government intends to ____________________ (A) federal governance of water resources towards long-term water security.

 Q1. What could be the appropriate title of this passage?
solution: Refer to the last and second last paragraph of this passage, it states that crisis of water is not due to scarcity but it is due to lack of preservation measures for delivering the same. As only groundwater is not sufficient due to expanding urbanisation, there needs to be long term planning and alongside staying prepared for drought. Also, in the last paragraph, the author says for reconsidering the strategies for water governance. For coping up with water security challenges, the Centre needs to collaborate with States strengthening the water resources governance and ensuring water security in the long term. Rest of the options are not specific enough to portray the passage as a whole. Thus, option (d) is the most suitable title for the above passage

For almost two decades, the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) has been reporting on the increasing number of over-exploited blocks across India, the ‘dark’ category blocks. The recent annual book of CGWB has reported 1,034 units, out of the 6,584 units it monitors, as over-exploited. If this is the ‘crisis’, then we have had it for long. What has this not received enough attention? Is it because these zones are not in cities?

Just to be sure how critical the ‘crisis’ is, CGWB’s 2013 estimates say that the groundwater development in India is just about 62% of the utilisable groundwater reserves. Similarly, a recent report by the Central Water Commission, prepared in collaboration with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), asserted that India is not yet in “water scarcity condition”. But it is certainly in a “water-stressed condition”, with reducing per capita water availability. Here, we certainly don’t mean to say that India can continue with the present ways of water management. We also cannot remain in a state of denial that a crisis is not in the making. However, certain steps need to be taken to ensure a more useful and productive discourse about water governance challenges.

First, India needs to reconsider the institutional processes for dissemination of knowledge about water resource management. There is a certain amount of danger inherent in the casual manner in which knowledge about water resources is legitimised and consumed, particularly in these days of ‘viral’ information.

Second, we need to recognise the crisis is not as much of scarcity as of delivery. The challenge is to ensure an adequate access to quality water, more so in urban areas where inequities over space and time are acute. We need to also realise that with the country’s rapid urbanisation, demand cannot be met by groundwater reserves alone. For instance, according to the Delhi Jal Board estimates, groundwater meets just 10% of Delhi’s drinking water needs. The rest is met by surface water sources, most of it transported from outside Delhi. The urban needs, which underpin much reporting on ‘water crises’, need to be met by robust long-term planning and preparation for droughts and other contingencies.

Finally, we need to reconsider our approaches to water governance. We must recognise that the fulcrum of change and action is with the States. For long, water resource departments in States have continued to follow the conventional approaches of supply augmentation. The challenge is that of reorienting themselves towards deploying strategies of demand management, conservation and regulation. The Centre has to work with States towards an institutional change for the necessary course-shift. The Finance Minister, in her budget, repeatedly stated that the government will work with States to address India’s national water security challenges. Let us hope that the government intends to ____________________ (A) federal governance of water resources towards long-term water security.

Q3. As per the passage, what are the steps taken to ensure maximum fulfilment of water governance?
options: Spreading the knowledge about water resource management
Providing adequate access to quality water
Changing the conventional approaches of supply augmentation
answer: Option D: All of the above
solution: Refer to the, third, fourth and fifth paragraph of the above passage, the steps necessary to reach maximum results fulfilling challenges of water governance are given. Hence, option (d) is the right answer choice

question:
Directions (6-10): Read the given passage and answer the following questions based on the passage.
There has been much development recently with respect to the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012. With an objective of stopping the rampant sexual abuse of children, the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (Amendment) Bill, 2019 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha in July, and later passed by both Houses of Parliament. It is all set to become the ‘law of the land’. The present bill is welcome in certain respects as it specifically defines what ‘child pornography’ is; ‘using a child for pornographic purposes’ and for ‘possessing or storing pornography involving a child’ is punishable. It has also widened the ambit of ‘Aggravated sexual assault’.

The highlight of the Bill is the introduction of the death penalty for the rape of minors. The Bill, in its object clause, justifies this by referring to the judgments of the Supreme Court in Machhi Singh (1983) and Devender Pal Singh (2002) in which the court has held that the death penalty can be awarded only in rarest of rare cases. Thus the intention of the Bill is to have a deterrent effect; but it can be argued that the introduction of the death penalty may backfire in cases of child sexual abuse and even have a catastrophic effect. Often, the perpetrators of abuse are family members and having such penalty in the statute book may discourage the registration of the crime itself. Also, it may threaten the life of the minor as the maximum punishment for murder is also the death sentence.

The Justice J.S. Verma Committee, which was constituted in 2013 in the aftermath of the Nirbhaya case, after due deliberations found itself against the imposition of death penalty in rape cases. The 262nd Report of the Law Commission of India, 2015, also provides for abolition of the death penalty except in terror cases.
Today, the death penalty has become a prominent tool of symbolic legislation — a political statement indeed. Many a time, the Government, by introducing the death penalty, portrays itself to be strict and serious with regard to such offences. It largely diverts attention from the core issues of infrastructural apathy, procedural lapses and trial delays and conveniently evades the fact that ‘it is the certainty of punishment rather than its severity which has deterrence in real sense’. It is pertinent to note here that even a year-and-a-half after the passage of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill, 2018, which introduced the death penalty for rape of a minor girl, such incidents have not been under check. The debate here is not about retaining or abolishing the death penalty but the probable _________________________(A) of its provision in the Act.

The Supreme Court has recently taken cognisance of the sexual abuse of children, directing its registry to file a case as writ petition with cause title “In-re Alarming Rise in The Number of Reported Child Rape Incidents”. The court has also observed that it intends having a ‘zero tolerance policy’ toward child rape. As data on sexual crimes against children collected by the court show, 24,212 FIRs were filed across India from January to June this year. According to National Crime Records Bureau data of 2016, the conviction rate in POCSO cases is 29.6% while pendency is as high as 89%. The prescribed time period of two months for trial in such cases is hardly complied with.

The court has also taken note of the delay in trials, in turn directing the Central Government to set up special courts within 60 days of the order in each district having more than 100 pending cases under the Act. It is to be seen how long it takes to comply with the order.
The Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2018 introduced the death penalty for rape of girls below the age of 12. At the same time, the POCSO Act, under Section 42, provides that where the same act constitutes an offence under the said Act and any other law, then the offender will be punished under the Act or such law, whichever provides for greater punishment. This has created an issue as the effect of such an amendment was death penalty for rape of minor girls but not for assault against minor boys.

The proposed Bill does away with such a discrepancy. It is gender neutral and provides for the death penalty for “aggravated penetrative sexual assault of a child”, thus bringing both these pieces of legislation on a par with each other in this respect. With these amendments and with the Supreme Court considering child abuse “intolerable”, there seems to be reasonable hope now that vulnerable children could be safer. The Bill is a step forward in preventing child abuse but the consequences of providing for the death penalty need to be closely observed.

 Q6. What could be the most appropriate title of this passage?
options: Diverting attention from core issues under POSCO Bill
answer: Option A: Pondering over POSCO Bill
solution: Option (a) is the most suitable answer choice. It fits as the title of the passage because it states the entire theme behind this passage in few and precise words.

Yet, when it comes to wage revision, the question of profitability arise. The settlement takes place between Indian Banks’ Association (IBA) and United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU).

The IBA represents bank managements and the UFBU, officers, employees, and staff organisations. The Charter of demands had been submitted in a time bound manner and the IBA had agreed to complete the process of negotiations expeditiously within the time-frame so as to reach the settlement before October 2017. paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
Statements: All engineers are coders. Some coders are testers. No tester is a manager. 
Conclusions: I. Some coders are not managers. II. Some engineers are testers. III. No engineer is a manager.
solution: Statement I: All engineers are coders, Some coders are testers, No tester is a manager. The subset of coders who are testers cannot be managers; hence 'Some coders are not managers' follows definitively. II (Some engineers are testers) does not necessarily follow as the circle of engineers may not overlap with testers. III (No engineer is a manager) does not necessarily follow. Thus, only conclusion I follows.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
Statements: Some pens are books. All books are chairs. No chair is a table. 
Conclusions: I. Some pens are chairs. II. No book is a table. III. Some pens are not tables. IV. Some tables are 
pens.
solution:
Statements: Some pens are books. All books are chairs. No chair is a table.
- Conclusion I: Some pens are chairs. Since some pens are books and all books are chairs, pens overlapping books must also overlap chairs. (Follows)
- Conclusion II: No book is a table. Since all books are inside chairs and no chair is a table, books cannot overlap tables. (Follows)
- Conclusion III: Some pens are not tables. The pens that are chairs cannot be tables. (Follows)
- Conclusion IV: Some tables are pens. No positive overlap between tables and pens is guaranteed. (Does not follow)
Therefore, I, II and III only follow.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
Data Sufficiency. For integers x and y, is x > y? 
I. x² > y². II. x + y > 0.

options.C: Both together are sufficient, neither alone
options.D:
Even both 
together are not sufficient

correct_answer_text: Both together are sufficient, neither alone
solution:
Question: Is x > y for integers x and y?
- Statement I: x² > y² gives |x| > |y|. If x = -3, y = 2, x² = 9 > 4 but x < y. If x = 3, y = 2, x > y. Insufficient.
- Statement II: x + y > 0 gives x > -y. If x = -1, y = 3, x < y. If x = 3, y = -1, x > y. Insufficient.
- Both together: x² > y² => x² - y² > 0 => (x - y)(x + y) > 0. Since Statement II guarantees (x + y) > 0, we can safely divide both sides by (x + y) without changing the inequality sign, yielding (x - y) > 0, which means x > y! Definite YES. Both together are sufficient, neither alone.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
Data Sufficiency. What is Riya's present age? 
I. Riya is twice as old as her sister, who is 3 years younger than their brother. 
II. Five years hence, the sum of the ages of Riya and her sister will be 40.

options.C: Both together are sufficient, neither alone
options.D:
Even both 
together are not sufficient

correct_answer_text: Both together are sufficient, neither alone
solution:
Question: What is Riya's present age?
- Statement I: R = 2S, S = B - 3. Three unknowns, two equations. Insufficient.
- Statement II: (R + 5) + (S + 5) = 40 => R + S = 30. Two unknowns, one equation. Insufficient.
- Both together: Substitute R = 2S into R + S = 30 => 2S + S = 30 => 3S = 30 => S = 10. Thus R = 20 years. Riya's present age is uniquely determined as 20. Both statements together are sufficient, neither alone.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text: In a certain code, MONDAY is written as NNOCBX. How is SUNDAY written in that code?
solution:
Coding Pattern: M (+1) -> N, O (-1) -> N, N (+1) -> O, D (-1) -> C, A (+1) -> B, Y (-1) -> X. The alternating shift pattern is [+1, -1, +1, -1, +1, -1].
Applying to SUNDAY:
- S (+1) -> T
- U (-1) -> T
- N (+1) -> O
- D (-1) -> C
- A (+1) -> B
- Y (-1) -> X
Result: TTOCBX.

question_text:
In a code, "sun rises early" = "ka mo ti", "early bird catches" = "ti ra po", and "bird sun light" = "ra ka du". 
What is the code for "rises bird light"?
solution:
Word-code comparison:
1) 'sun rises early' = 'ka mo ti'
2) 'early bird catches' = 'ti ra po' => Common word 'early' = 'ti'.
3) 'bird sun light' = 'ra ka du' => Compare (1) & (3): common word 'sun' = 'ka'.
From (1), remaining word 'rises' = 'mo'.
Compare (2) & (3): common word 'bird' = 'ra'.
From (3), remaining word 'light' = 'du'.
Target: 'rises bird light' = 'mo ra du'.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
A solid cube painted red on all faces is cut into 64 identical small cubes (4 × 4 × 4). How many small 
cubes have exactly two faces painted?
solution:
For an n × n × n painted cube cut into unit cubes (here n = 4 since 4³ = 64):
Cubes with exactly two faces painted lie along the 12 edges (excluding the 2 corner cubes on each edge):
Number = 12 × (n - 2) = 12 × (4 - 2) = 12 × 2 = 24.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
In triangle ABC, the medians AD, BE and CF are drawn and meet at G. How many triangles are there in 
the figure in total?
solution:
Standard median geometry counting:
In triangle ABC with medians AD, BE, CF intersecting at centroid G:
1) 6 small elementary triangles formed around centroid G: AFG, BFG, BDG, CDG, CEG, AEG.
2) 3 triangles formed by pairing two adjacent elementary triangles opposite vertices: ABG, BCG, CAG.
3) 6 triangles formed by combining three elementary triangles (split by each median into halves): ABD, ACD, BCE, ABE, CAF, CBF.
4) 1 whole outer triangle: ABC.
Total = 6 + 3 + 6 + 1 = 16 triangles.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
If A + B means A is the mother of B, A − B means A is the brother of B, and A × B means A is the father 
of B, which expression shows that P is the maternal uncle of R?
solution:
P must be the maternal uncle of R (brother of R's mother).
- Q + R means Q is the mother of R.
- P - Q means P is the brother of Q.
Combining them: P - Q + R means P is the brother of Q (who is the mother of R), so P is R's maternal uncle.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
Ravi walks 10 m north, turns right and walks 6 m, turns right and walks 14 m, turns left and walks 3 m, 
then turns left and walks 4 m. Where is he now relative to the starting point?
solution:
Step-by-step vector tracking from origin (0, 0):
1) Walks 10 m North -> (0, 10)
2) Turns right (East) and walks 6 m -> (6, 10)
3) Turns right (South) and walks 14 m -> (6, 10 - 14) = (6, -4)

question_text: In how many ways can the letters of COMMITTEE be arranged so that no two vowels are adjacent?
solution:
Word COMMITTEE contains 9 letters: C(1), O(1), M(2), I(1), T(2), E(2).
Vowels: O, I, E, E (4 vowels, with two E's).
Consonants: C, M, M, T, T (5 consonants, with two M's and two T's).
1) Arrange the 5 consonants first:
   Number of ways = 5! / (2! × 2!) = 120 / 4 = 30 ways.
2) 5 consonants create 6 available gaps: _ C _ M _ M _ T _ T _
   To ensure no two vowels are adjacent, choose 4 gaps out of 6 for the 4 vowels:
   C(6, 4) = 15 ways.
3) Arrange the 4 vowels (O, I, E, E) in the chosen 4 gaps:
   Number of ways = 4! / 2! = 24 / 2 = 12 ways.
Total arrangements = 30 × 15 × 12 = 5,400.

is the probability that all three are of different colours?
solution:

solution:

Marked Price (MP) = 100 × 1.40 = 140.
Successive discounts of 10% and 15%:
Selling Price (SP) = 140 × (1 - 0.10) × (1 - 0.15) = 140 × 0.90 × 0.85 = 126 × 0.85 = 107.1.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
A, B and C can individually finish a job in 12, 18 and 24 days respectively. They work on alternate days 
in the order A, B, C, A, B, C, … (one person per day, starting with A). On which day is the job completed?
solution:
Let total work = LCM(12, 18, 24) = 72 units.
Daily efficiencies:
- A = 72 / 12 = 6 units/day
- B = 72 / 18 = 4 units/day
- C = 72 / 24 = 3 units/day
They work on alternate days: A on Day 1, B on Day 2, C on Day 3, A on Day 4, etc.
In 1 cycle of 3 days, work done = 6 + 4 + 3 = 13 units.
In 5 full cycles (15 days), work done = 5 × 13 = 65 units.
Remaining work = 72 - 65 = 7 units.
- Day 16: A works and completes 6 units. Total work = 65 + 6 = 71 units. Remaining = 1 unit.
- Day 17: B works. Since B does 4 units/day, B finishes the remaining 1 unit in 1/4 of a day.
Therefore, the job is completed on the 17th day.

Two trains of lengths 240 m and 160 m run on parallel tracks. Running in opposite directions they cross 
each other in 8 s; running in the same direction the faster overtakes the slower in 40 s. The speed of the 
faster train is:
solution:
Total distance to clear = 240 m + 160 m = 400 m.
Let speed of faster train = v1 m/s and slower train = v2 m/s.
1) Running in opposite directions, relative speed = v1 + v2 = 400 / 8 = 50 m/s.
2) Running in same direction, relative speed = v1 - v2 = 400 / 40 = 10 m/s.
Adding the two equations: 2·v1 = 60 => v1 = 30 m/s.
Converting to km/h: 30 × (18 / 5) = 108 km/h.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 1
question_text:
In an election, 20,000 voters were registered. 80% voted, and 5% of the votes cast were invalid. The 
winner got 55% of the valid votes. By how many votes did he win?
solution:
Total registered voters = 20,000.
Voters who voted = 80% of 20,000 = 16,000.
Invalid votes = 5% of 16,000 = 800.
Valid votes = 16,000 - 800 = 15,200.
Winner obtained 55% of valid votes => Loser obtained (100% - 55%) = 45%.
Winning margin = 55% - 45% = 10% of valid votes.
Winning margin = 0.10 × 15,200 = 1,520 votes.

The difference between compound interest (annual) and simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 10% 
p.a. is ₹310. Find the sum.
solution:
Difference between CI and SI for 3 years at rate r%:
Formula: Difference = P × (r / 100)² × (3 + r / 100).
Given r = 10% and Difference = ₹310:
310 = P × (0.10)² × (3 + 0.10)
310 = P × 0.01 × 3.10 = P × 0.031
P = 310 / 0.031 = ₹10,000.

In software organisations, "technical debt" is often treated as a purely engineering concern, a messy 
residue of hurried decisions that developers will eventually tidy up. This framing is misleading. Debt, in

be acting shrewdly. The problem arises when the interest, meaning the extra effort every future change 
demands, is never acknowledged on the balance sheet. Teams then find that features which once took 
days now take weeks, yet managers, seeing only the delivered functionality, attribute the slowdown to 
declining developer productivity. Proponents of disciplined refactoring argue that a fixed share of every 
sprint should be reserved for repayment. Critics counter that such quotas are arbitrary and encourage 
cosmetic rewrites that leave real risks untouched. A more defensible approach, some suggest, is to make 
debt visible by tracking how often particular modules cause delays or defects, and to repay only where 
the interest is demonstrably high.

solution:
Let sum invested at 8% SI = ₹x.
Then sum invested at 10% CI = ₹(12,000 - x).
Time = 2 years.
- Simple Interest at 8% for 2 years = (x × 8 × 2) / 100 = 0.16x.
- Compound Interest at 10% for 2 years = (12,000 - x) × [(1 + 0.10)² - 1] = (12,000 - x) × 0.21 = 2,520 - 0.21x.
Total interest = 0.16x + 2,520 - 0.21x = 2,520 - 0.05x.
Given total interest = ₹2,270:
2,520 - 0.05x = 2,270
0.05x = 250
x = 250 / 0.05 = ₹5,000.

solution:
Take CP = 100 per unit weight, so marked price = 125 (25% intended profit). After a 12% discount, SP 
= 125 × 0.88 = 110. But he delivers only 0.9 units (10% short weight) whose true cost is 90. Profit = 110 − 90 =

A and B together can complete a task in 15 days. They worked together for 5 days, after which A left 
and B completed the remaining work alone in 20 more days. In how many days can A alone complete the 
task?
solution:
In 5 days together, they finish 5/15 = 1/3. The remaining 2/3 is done by B alone in 20 days, so B's rate 
= (2/3)/20 = 1/30/day (B alone takes 30 days). Combined rate = 1/15, so A's rate = 1/15 − 1/30 = 1/30/day — 
A alone also takes 30 days.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 3
question_text:
Statements: All P are Q. All Q are R. Some R are S. No S is T. 
Conclusions: I. All P are R. II. Some Q are S. III. No P is T. IV. Some R are not T.
solution:
Since P⊆Q⊆R, "All P are R" (I) follows directly. Some R are S, and no S is T, so those particular R-
elements are not T — "Some R are not T" (IV) follows. Neither II nor III can be derived, since we don't know 
how P or Q specifically relates to the R-elements that happen to be S.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 3
question_text:
Data Sufficiency. What is the two-digit number N? 
I. The sum of its digits is 9. 
II. The number obtained by reversing its digits is 27 less than N.

options.A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but II alone is not
options.B: Statement II alone is sufficient, but I alone is not
options.C: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
options.D:
Each statement alone is sufficient 
(e) Even both statements together are not sufficient

correct_answer_text: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
solution:
II alone: N − reversed = 9(tens digit − units digit) = 27, so tens − units = 3 — multiple numbers fit (41, 
52, 63, 74, 85, 96), insufficient alone. I alone: digit sum = 9 also fits multiple numbers, insufficient alone. 
Together: tens − units = 3 and tens + units = 9 gives tens = 6, units = 3, so N = 63 — unique.

A man walks 12 m North, then 9 m East, then 8 m South, then 6 m West. How far is he from the starting 
point, and in which general direction?
solution:
Net North-South displacement = 12−8 = 4 m North; net East-West = 9−6 = 3 m East. Distance = 
√(3²+4²) = √25 = 5 m, in the general North-East direction.

In how many ways can 8 different books be distributed among 3 students so that one student gets 4

Bag A has 4 red and 6 black balls; Bag B has 7 red and 3 black balls. A bag is chosen at random and one

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 3
question_text:
A dealer's cost price for a mixture of two rice varieties (mixed 3:2 by weight at ₹40/kg and ₹60/kg) 
works out to ₹48/kg. He marks up the price by 25% and sells it, but uses a false weight that gives only 900 g 
for every 1 kg paid for. Find his actual profit percentage.
solution:
Marked-up SP for a claimed 1 kg = 48×1.25 = ₹60. True cost of the 900 g actually given = 0.9×48 = 
₹43.2. Profit = 60−43.2 = ₹16.8 on a true cost of ₹43.2, giving 16.8/43.2×100 ≈ 38.9%.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 3
question_text:
Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours, Pipe B in 15 hours, and a leak can empty the full tank in 20 hours. All 
three are opened together for 4 hours, after which the leak is plugged. How much more time do A and B 
together need to fill the remaining tank?
solution:
Combined rate (A+B−leak) = 1/12+1/15−1/20 = 5/60+4/60−3/60 = 1/10 per hour. In 4 hours, 4/10 = 
2/5 of the tank fills, leaving 3/5. A+B's combined rate (no leak) = 1/12+1/15 = 3/20 per hour. Time for 
remaining 3/5 = (3/5)÷(3/20) = 4 hours.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 3
question_text:
In a 1000 m race, A beats B by 100 m, and in a separate 1000 m race, B beats C by 100 m (each runner 
maintains a constant speed across races). By how many metres does A beat C in a 1000 m race between 
them?
solution:
Speed ratio A:B = 1000:900 = 10:9 (A beats B by 100 m in 1000 m). Similarly B:C = 10:9. So A:C = 
(10/9)×(10/9) = 100:81. When A covers 1000 m, C covers (81/100)×1000 = 810 m. A beats C by 1000−810 = 
190 m.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 3
question_text:
Write a short technical essay/paragraph of 150–180 words. 
Explain, in your own words, the trade-offs between vertical scaling (upgrading a single server's capacity) and 
horizontal scaling (adding more servers) of a server infrastructure. Recommend which approach a mid-sized 
e-commerce company experiencing rapid, unpredictable traffic growth should adopt, and justify your 
recommendation. 

 
 
Evaluation rubric (10 marks): Technical accuracy of the comparison (3) | Clarity of the recommendation and 
justification (3) | Structure and coherence (2) | Grammar and vocabulary (1) | Word limit adherence (1)
solution:
Evaluation Rubric (10 Marks): Technical accuracy & depth (3) | Structural coherence (3) | Trade-off synthesis (2) | Grammar & style (1) | Word limit (1)

Model Response:
When architecting scalable enterprise systems, engineers must weigh the fundamental trade-offs between vertical scaling (scaling up) and horizontal scaling (scaling out). 

Vertical scaling enhances system capacity by upgrading existing hardware with faster processors, additional RAM, or expanded NVMe storage. Its primary advantage lies in architectural simplicity: monolithic codebases require zero modification, data consistency is effortlessly preserved within a single memory space, and network latency between distributed nodes is entirely eliminated. However, vertical scaling faces strict physical ceiling limits, exhibits exponentially rising costs at high-tier configurations, and inherently introduces a single point of failure during hardware maintenance.

In contrast, horizontal scaling expands throughput by distributing traffic across multiple commodity instances behind load balancers. While this approach provides virtually limitless linear scalability, elastic cost management, and superior fault tolerance, it significantly increases operational complexity. Systems must handle network partitions, implement distributed data synchronization (such as eventual consistency), and manage distributed tracing. Consequently, mature architectures often scale vertically in early development before decomposing into horizontally scalable, resilient distributed microservices.

question_text:
Statements: Some pens are pencils. All pencils are erasers. No eraser is a sharpener. 
Conclusions: I. No pencil is a sharpener. II. Some pens are erasers. III. Some erasers are not pens. IV. Either 
some pens are sharpeners or no pens are sharpeners.
solution:
Pencils⊆erasers and erasers∩sharpeners=∅, so pencils∩sharpeners=∅ (I follows). Some pens are 
pencils, and pencils⊆erasers, so some pens are erasers (II follows). III isn't guaranteed (no information 
ensures an eraser outside the pen-pencil overlap exists). For IV: we know the pen-pencils aren't sharpeners, 
but nothing is said about pens that aren't pencils, so neither "some pens are sharpeners" nor "no pens are 
sharpeners" can be individually proven — exactly the condition for the standard either-or rule, so IV follows.

Distributed systems theory offers a deceptively simple trilemma: a system cannot simultaneously 
guarantee consistency, availability and partition tolerance, and must therefore sacrifice one when a 
network partition occurs. In practice, however, the theorem is more often invoked than correctly applied, 
because partition tolerance is not actually optional for any system whose nodes communicate over an 
unreliable network, which is to say nearly all distributed systems built today. The real choice, once 
partition tolerance is accepted as a structural necessity rather than a design preference, is between 
consistency and availability during the partition itself, and this choice need not be uniform across an 
entire system. A payment ledger might reasonably refuse writes during a partition to preserve 
consistency, accepting temporary unavailability as the lesser cost, while a product catalogue serving read 
traffic might instead continue answering requests with potentially stale data, judging availability the 
more valuable property for that workload. Treating the CAP theorem as prescribing a single, system-wide 

choice, rather than a per-operation or per-service one, is therefore a common and consequential 
misreading.

How many swaps are performed in total?

swaps = 0 
for i = 0 to 4

solution:
7. Full bubble-sort trace: pass i=0 gives 3 swaps (array becomes [2,5,1,8,3,9]); pass i=1 gives 2 more 
swaps ([2,1,5,3,8,9]); pass i=2 gives 2 more swaps ([1,2,3,5,8,9], now sorted); passes i=3 and i=4 give 0

question_text:
This algorithm reverses the first k elements of a queue using a stack. What is printed? 
queue = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] 
stack = [] 
k = 3 
for i = 1 to k 
    push(stack, dequeue(queue)) 
end for 
while (stack is not empty) 
    enqueue(queue, pop(stack)) 
end while 
for i = 1 to (5 - k) 
    enqueue(queue, dequeue(queue)) 
end for 
print(queue)
solution:
This is the standard "reverse first k of a queue" algorithm. After moving the first 3 elements through 
the stack, the queue becomes [4,5,3,2,1]; the final rotation step (dequeue+enqueue twice) moves 4 and 5 to 
the back, giving [3,2,1,4,5] — the first 3 elements correctly reversed.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 4
question_text:
Write a short technical essay/paragraph of 150–180 words. 
A legacy monolithic application your team supports is becoming difficult to maintain and scale. Explain the 
key risks of migrating it to a microservices architecture versus keeping it monolithic but modularising the 
codebase internally, and recommend one approach for a team of 8 engineers with limited DevOps 
experience, justifying your choice. 
Evaluation rubric (10 marks): Technical accuracy of the comparison (3) | Clarity and soundness of the 
recommendation given the team's constraints (3) | Structure and coherence (2) | Grammar and vocabulary 
(1) | Word limit adherence (1)
solution:
Evaluation Rubric (10 Marks): Technical accuracy (3) | Risk analysis (3) | Phasing justification (2) | Vocabulary & grammar (1) | Word limit (1)

Model Response:
Decomposing a legacy monolithic system into microservices offers compelling advantages in modularity and independent continuous deployment. However, for an engineering team of eight developers with limited DevOps maturity, a sudden, wholesale migration introduces grave systemic risks. 

The primary danger is replacing simple in-process memory calls with distributed network communication, which introduces network latency, partial failure modes, and distributed data consistency challenges. Without sophisticated infrastructure for service discovery, container orchestration, and centralized telemetry, operational overhead will quickly overwhelm a small team, stalling feature delivery.

A far more defensible, risk-mitigated strategy is phased internal modularization. The team should first refactor the monolith into a 'modular monolith' with strictly enforced package boundaries, clear interface contracts, and decoupled database schemas. This achieves clean code maintainability and testability without distributed systems operational overhead. Once the team establishes automated CI/CD pipelines, container monitoring, and robust integration testing, high-traffic domain boundaries can be incrementally extracted into standalone microservices using the Strangler Fig pattern.

question_text:
Data Sufficiency. If x and y are positive integers, what is the remainder when x is divided by y? 
I. x = 5y + 3 
II. y = 7

options.A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but II alone is not
options.B: Statement II alone is sufficient, but I alone is not
options.C: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
options.D: Even both statements together are not sufficient

correct_answer_text: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
solution:
I alone: x=5y+3 only gives remainder 3 if y>3; for small y (e.g., y=2, x=13, 13÷2 leaves remainder 1, not 
3) it fails — insufficient alone. II alone: y=7 with x unknown is insufficient. Together: x=5(7)+3=38, and 38÷7 
leaves remainder 3 (valid since 3<7) — sufficient together.

I. A is twice as efficient as B. 
II. A alone can complete the job in 12 days.

options.A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but II alone is not
options.B: Statement II alone is sufficient, but I alone is not
options.C: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
options.D: Even both statements together are not sufficient

correct_answer_text: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
solution:
II alone gives only A's rate (1/12), with B's rate unknown. I alone gives only a ratio (2:1), with no 
absolute rate. Together: A's rate=1/12, B's rate=1/24 (half of A's), combined rate=1/12+1/24=3/24=1/8, so 
together they take 8 days — sufficient together.

A rectangular cuboid is cut by 2 parallel cuts along its length, 1 cut along its breadth, and 3 cuts along its 
height (each cut perpendicular to that dimension), producing smaller cuboids from an originally fully-painted 
surface. How many of the resulting small cuboids have exactly 1 painted face?
solution:
With 2 cuts in length (3 pieces), 1 cut in breadth (2 pieces), 3 cuts in height (4 pieces), every piece 
touches an outer breadth-face (since there's no "middle" breadth layer). A piece has exactly 1 painted face 
only if it is interior in BOTH length and height (contributing 0 from each) while contributing exactly 1 from 
breadth (which is unavoidable). Interior length positions = 1 (out of 3), interior height positions = 2 (out of 4), 
and both breadth pieces qualify: 1×2×2 = 4.

Two runners start from the same point on a 600 m circular track at the same time, in opposite 
directions, at 8 m/s and 10 m/s. After how many seconds will they both simultaneously be back at the 
starting point for the first time?

LCM(75,60) = 300 s.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 5
question_text:
Write a short technical essay/paragraph of 150–180 words. 
Your team is choosing between two caching strategies for a high-traffic API: a write-through cache (data 
written to cache and database simultaneously) versus a write-back cache (data written to cache first, then 
asynchronously to the database). Explain the key trade-offs between these approaches in terms of data 
consistency and performance, and recommend which strategy best suits (a) a financial transactions API, and 
(b) a social media "like" counter — justifying each recommendation briefly. 
Evaluation rubric (10 marks): Technical accuracy of the trade-off explanation (3) | Soundness of both 
context-specific recommendations (3) | Structure and coherence (2) | Grammar and vocabulary (1) | Word 
limit adherence (1)
solution:
Evaluation Rubric (10 Marks): Architecture accuracy (3) | Trade-off comparison (3) | Recommendation logic (2) | Vocabulary (1) | Word limit (1)

Model Response:
Choosing the optimal caching topology for high-throughput APIs requires balancing latency, data consistency, and memory utilization between write-through and write-around (cache-aside) strategies.

In a write-through architecture, the application writes data simultaneously to both the cache and the primary persistent database. This ensures strict data freshness, virtually eliminating stale reads, and guarantees that newly committed records are instantly available in memory for immediate subsequent queries. However, write-through caching introduces higher initial write latency because each mutation requires two round-trips. Furthermore, it risks cache pollution if written data is rarely requested again before being evicted by memory pressure.

Conversely, a write-around strategy bypasses the cache entirely during write operations, storing updates directly into the database. Data is loaded into the cache lazily only upon an initial cache miss. This approach minimizes write latency and protects cache memory from rarely read data. Nevertheless, it incurs higher read latency on subsequent queries and requires explicit TTL expiration or invalidation logic to prevent stale reads in read-heavy workloads.

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 6
question_text:
Statements: Some bugs are features. All features are releases. No release is stable. All patches are 
stable. 
Conclusions: I. Some bugs are not stable. II. No patch is a feature. III. Some releases are bugs. IV. Some stable 
things are bugs.
solution:
Some bugs are features, features are releases, and no release is stable — so those bugs are not stable 
(I). Patches⊆stable and features∩stable=∅ (features are releases), so no patch is a feature (II). Some bugs 
are releases, which converts to "some releases are bugs" (III). IV does not follow: the only bugs we know are 
unstable; nothing says any bug is stable.

If P # Q means P is the mother of Q, P $ Q means P is the brother of Q, and P @ Q means P is the wife of 
Q, then in the expression A $ B # C @ D, how is A related to D?
solution:
A is the brother of B, and B is the mother of C, so A is C's maternal uncle. C is the wife of D, so A is D's 
wife's maternal uncle — an uncle-in-law.

question_text:
A is 20 km due North of B. C is 15 km due East of B. What is the bearing of A from C (measured clockwise 
from North, to the nearest degree)?
solution:
Taking East and North as axes, A is at (0,20), B at (0,0), C at (15,0). The vector from C to A is (−15, 20): 
36.87° west of north, giving a bearing of 360°−36.87° ≈ 323°.

   tan(∠ACB) = AB / BC = 20 / 15 = 4/3 => ∠ACB ≈ 53.13°
   Bearing of A from C = 360° - (90° + 53.13°) = 307° (or N 53° W).

question_text:
Three fair dice are rolled. Given that at least one die shows a 6, what is the probability that the sum of 
the three dice is 12?
solution:
Outcomes with at least one 6: 6³−5³ = 91. Of these, the sum is 12 in 15 outcomes (permutations of

question_text:
A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects the disease in 95% of those who have it, but also 
gives a false positive for 10% of those who do not. If a randomly chosen person tests positive, what is the 
probability that they actually have the disease?
solution:
P(disease and positive) = 0.01×0.95 = 0.0095; P(no disease and positive) = 0.99×0.10 = 0.099. 
P(disease | positive) = 0.0095/0.1085 = 19/217 (≈ 8.8%).

paper_name: Infosys System Engineer ITM Mock Paper 6
question_text:
A 180 m long train passes a man walking at 6 km/h in the same direction in 12 seconds. How long will 
this train take to completely cross a 420 m long platform?
solution:
Relative speed = 180/12 = 15 m/s = 54 km/h; the train's speed = 54+6 = 60 km/h = 50/3 m/s. Time to 
cross the platform = (180+420)/(50/3) = 36 s.

Subject: Security Advisory: Production Vulnerability Identification and Immediate Remediation Plan

Dear Ms. Thornton,

During our routine internal security audit of the production customer portal this morning, our team identified a critical vulnerability involving insecure direct object references (IDOR) within the invoice retrieval API endpoint.

If maliciously exploited, this flaw could permit an authenticated user to view billing records belonging to other corporate accounts by manipulating URL parameters. Our preliminary forensic log analysis indicates that no unauthorized data exfiltration or external access has occurred.

To ensure immediate protection, our team has deployed a temporary Web Application Firewall (WAF) rule at 11:30 AM today that validates parameter ownership and blocks cross-account requests. question_text:
Statements: Some servers are clients. All clients are nodes. No node is offline. Some offline things are 
routers. 
Conclusions: I. Some servers are not offline. II. Some routers are not nodes. III. No client is a router. IV. Some 
nodes are servers.
solution:
Some servers are clients and clients are nodes, which are never offline, so those servers are not offline 
(I). Some offline things are routers, and nodes are never offline, so those routers are not nodes (II). Some 
servers are nodes, which converts to "some nodes are servers" (IV). III does not follow, because other 
routers (not the offline ones) might be clients.

Read the passage and answer Q26–30. 
In distributed systems, a network call that times out leaves the caller in genuine ignorance: the request 
may have been lost before reaching the server, executed successfully with the reply lost on the way back, 
or still be in flight. Retrying is the natural response, but retrying a non-idempotent operation — charging 
a card, say — risks performing it twice. The standard remedy is to make the operation idempotent by 
attaching a unique request identifier, so that the server can recognise a duplicate and return the original 
result instead of re-executing. This shifts the burden rather than removing it: the server must now durably 
remember identifiers, and must decide how long to remember them, since storing them forever is costly 
while discarding them too early reopens the window for duplicates. Engineers who treat idempotency as 
a mere implementation detail therefore tend to discover it as an incident, whereas those who treat it as 
part of an operation's contract design it in from the start.

300 and 360 minutes: 7 times.

Model Response:
Load balancing algorithms are fundamental to distributed systems resilience, determining how inbound network traffic is allocated across heterogeneous application server clusters. Two foundational Layer 4 and Layer 7 routing strategies are Round Robin and Least Connections.

Round Robin distributes incoming requests sequentially across available back-end servers in a static, cyclic rotation. Because it operates statelessly without querying server telemetry, Round Robin incurs virtually zero computational overhead. However, it operates on the flawed assumption that all requests impose identical processing burdens and that all servers process tasks at identical speeds. When requests vary significantly in execution duration, Round Robin can inadvertently overwhelm a server with concurrent long-running queries while adjacent nodes remain underutilized.

Conversely, the Least Connections algorithm dynamically tracks active client sessions on each instance, directing each new request to the server currently handling the fewest active connections. For services characterized by unpredictable request durations—such as data processing or complex report generation—Least Connections is distinctly superior, as it continuously self-balances server load and prevents cascading node exhaustion.
